note: Grok Direction C, named as deferred in decision 0202 Q3 and picked up here. Any input that normalizes to the empty string shares the same key as every other empty-norm input, so a store that accepts empty-norm rows treats its per-domain uniqueness constraint as last-writer-wins. This adds a boundary refusal — ``add_pair`` raises ``EmptyNormError`` at write time — with an explicit ``override_empty_norm=True`` escape hatch for a caller that genuinely wants the collision-prone key.

decisions.question: Should ``memory.add_pair`` refuse to write a pair whose ``source_text`` normalizes to the empty string?
decisions.commitment: Yes. `nestor/memory.py` gains an `EmptyNormError` class (a `NestorError` subclass sitting alongside `ConflictingSealError`, `RejectedPairError`, etc.) and a boundary check in `add_pair` right after `norm = matcher.normalize(source_text)`: if `not norm` and `not override_empty_norm`, raise `EmptyNormError` naming the offending source_text, the matcher class, and the override path. The refusal happens BEFORE the ledger preflight, the conflict checks, and any store write, so no row lands and no ledger entry accumulates. Applies to sealed AND draft — the collision-prone key is the danger, and it doesn't care about sealing state. Gated by 20 tests in tests/test_refuse_empty_norm_seals.py covering pure punctuation, math symbols (∞), currency ($$$), whitespace, and empty string across sealed/draft, plus the override_empty_norm=True escape hatch and its still-collides behaviour. Two PR #180 tests that used to lock the old silent-empty-norm-sealing behaviour (test_empty_after_normalize, test_all_whitespace_source) are rewritten in place against the new refusal — same posture PR #217 took with the emoji tests.
decisions.why: The collision-prone class is real: pure punctuation, pure math symbols, pure whitespace, and pure emoji (before decision 0202) all collapsed to ``''`` under the default StringMatcher and shared the per-domain uniqueness slot. Grok's Part 2 recap ('🔥 started returning the 💀 translation') named it in the emoji case; the refusal here closes the whole class regardless of which specific input class the strip pass will collapse next. Refusing at the boundary makes the failure mode a visible error at write time rather than a silent overwrite that shows up as a wrong answer later — the seat rule about 'refuse before writing rather than repair after' applied to the write path. The override_empty_norm escape hatch is there for the same reason override_conflict is there for ConflictingSealError: a specific caller with a specific reason can accept responsibility for the collision, and the guard's job is to make sure the responsibility is explicit rather than accidental.

decisions.question: Should this land BEFORE or AFTER PR #217 (emoji preservation)?
decisions.commitment: After. This branch is stacked on `claude/pr180-emoji-normalize` (PR #217) rather than master. PR #217 rewrites the two emoji tests that used to seal `"🌍"` and `"❤️"` (which collapsed to `""` before the So/Sk preservation); without those rewrites, this PR's refuse-empty-norm would also refuse those seals and break PR #217's ordering. Stacking keeps the merge order clean: emoji fix lands first (which un-empties emoji), then this lands (which refuses whatever is still empty). Once #217 merges to master the base branch here can be retargeted to master.
decisions.why: The two changes are orthogonal in intent (0202 preserves emoji through normalize; 0204 refuses whatever normalize collapsed to empty) but coupled in tests: some PR #180 tests seal inputs that used to collapse to empty and now don't (emoji, covered by 0202) or still do (punctuation, math, whitespace — the 0204 refusal class). The stacking makes both PRs individually reviewable and lands in an order where each PR's tests pass on the branch that carries it. PR #216's multilingual seeds is also stacked on the same base for the same reason (Arabic seed depends on 0200's NFC); this is the same pattern.

decisions.question: Why an override_empty_norm parameter instead of a hard refusal?
decisions.commitment: The parameter exists but defaults to False (refusal is the normal path). No production caller is expected to pass override_empty_norm=True; the shipped seeds, the recipes, and the covenant path all produce non-empty norms for legitimate content. The override is a documented escape hatch matching the shape of `override_conflict` (ConflictingSealError) and `override_rejection` (RejectedPairError) so a specific caller who has a documented reason (a test asserting the previous collision behavior; a very rare deployment where an empty key IS the intended semantics) can proceed with the responsibility explicitly named in the code that does it.
decisions.why: Symmetric with the existing NestorError family: every refusal has an override sibling. The refusal is what makes the danger visible; the override is what keeps the API from being unusable for legitimate specialized cases. Removing the override would force every specialized caller to catch-and-repackage the exception, which reads worse and hides intent from a reader. Keeping the parameter but defaulting off gets the safety of the refusal for every default-shape caller while leaving the escape hatch documented and grep-able.
